strengths: Clear motivation and novel domain focus: It addresses semantic scene completion (SSC) specifically for legged/humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera, addressing unique challenges like gait-induced jitter and 360° continuity that are ignored by typical autonomous driving pipelines.

Tailored and effective technical designs: Each module is well-justified. Dual-Projection (DP-ER) handles polar/equator distortion, Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) balances Cartesian precision near-field with Cylindrical efficiency far-field, and Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) elegantly resolves motion jitter in 2D prior to quantization.

New panoramic occupancy benchmarks: The introduction of QuadOcc (real quadruped dataset with 360° LiDAR-grounded annotation) and Human360Occ (CARLA synthetic humanoid dataset) represents a major contribution to the robotics and 3D perception community.

Strong quantitative and qualitative performance: OneOcc consistently outperforms both vision-based and classic LiDAR-based baselines across multiple splits and lighting conditions, while keeping real-time inference speed (~14-19 FPS) on a single GPU.
weaknesses: Relatively large model size: At 101.76M parameters, the model is on the heavier side for deployment on standard low-power embedded computers typically found on smaller quadrupeds (like Jetson Orin NX/Nano).

Low resolution voxel grid: The current experiments are conducted on 64x64x8 and 128x128x16 voxel grids. It is unclear how the computational complexity and performance scale to larger or higher-resolution grids that might be required for fine-grained locomotion or manipulation.

Sensitivity to calibration: Given the severe vibrations of legged platforms, camera calibration parameters might drift. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of how robust the method is under perturbed or noisy extrinsic/intrinsic calibrations.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and under-explored domain in Semantic Scene Completion (SSC): panoramic perception specifically tailored for legged and humanoid robots subjected to gait-induced body jitter.

Introduces two valuable and distinct panoramic occupancy benchmarks: QuadOcc (real-world quadruped, first-person 360-degree data with semi-automatic ground truth) and Human360Occ (H3O, simulated human-ego CARLA dataset). These will be beneficial assets for the embodied AI and robotics communities.

The architectural design is well-motivated and physically-grounded: Dual-Projection Fusion (DP-ER) balances equirectangular and raw annular representation, while Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) combines Cartesian precision for near-field contacts with cylindrical-polar coordinates for far-field continuity.

Demonstrates strong performance, outperforming established vision-based baselines (e.g., MonoScene, SGN, OccFormer) and even competing with LiDAR-based models on the proposed benchmarks, supported by extensive ablation studies.
weaknesses: The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) assumes a simplified 2D translation offset ($Δ_s = (dx, dy)$) in the image/feature plane to correct for motion jitter. However, legged robot locomotion typically induces complex high-frequency 3D rotational oscillations (roll, pitch, yaw) that cause non-uniform, spatially varying distortions in panoramic/equirectangular views. The validity and limitations of this uniform 2D translation assumption are not sufficiently discussed.

High parameter count and computational footprint for real-world deployment: At 101.76M parameters and 14.3 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, the model is quite heavy. Real-world legged or humanoid platforms are highly payload- and power-constrained, typically running on edge computers (e.g., Jetson Orin/Thor). The feasibility and latency of executing such a large model alongside downstream navigation, localization, and control stacks on actual robotic edge hardware are not demonstrated.

The generation details and quality of the semi-automatic ground truth for the real QuadOcc dataset are somewhat brief. Given the challenges of multi-frame LiDAR aggregation under dynamic legged motion, further analysis regarding label noise, occlusion artifacts, and consistency would improve confidence in the benchmark.

The evaluation is restricted solely to the newly proposed panoramic datasets. While the focus on panoramic cameras is clear, evaluating on a standard non-panoramic baseline benchmark (or adapting standard models more rigorously) would help better calibrate the generalized performance of the proposed modules.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and highly practical problem: 3D semantic scene completion specifically tailored for legged/humanoid robots, which face severe gait-induced motion jitter and require full 360-degree awareness under tight compute/sensor budgets.

The introduction of Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) is an elegant, computationally lightweight, and plug-and-play solution to mitigate high-frequency motion jitter by correcting coordinate mapping before 3D lifting.

The Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) and Dual-Projection (DP-ER) modules are physically well-motivated, successfully leveraging both Cartesian/polar representations and equirectangular/raw formats to handle perspective distortion and range differences.

The paper contributes two valuable, diverse panoramic occupancy benchmarks: QuadOcc (real quadruped dataset with semi-automatic ground truth) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego dataset), which will benefit future research in embodied AI and robotic perception.
Outstanding experimental results on both benchmarks, outperforming established camera and LiDAR baselines, supported by detailed ablation studies and real-world latency profiling.
weaknesses: The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) assumes a global 2D translation (dx, dy) to compensate for gait jitter. Since actual body motion involves complex 3D rotations (roll/pitch/yaw) and translations, a global 2D shift is a simplified approximation that may not fully capture depth-dependent pixel displacements.

The paper assumes perfect static camera calibration. In real legged robot deployment, mechanical vibrations can cause extrinsic drift over time. The impact of calibration noise or mechanical drift on the proposed pipeline is not thoroughly analyzed.

It is unclear if a standard video stabilization pre-processing step (e.g., using onboard IMU data) would achieve a similar effect to the learned GDC. Comparing GDC with standard IMU-based or gyro-based image stabilization would help clarify its relative advantage.

strengths: Strong and novel motivation: The paper targets panoramic semantic scene completion (SSC) specifically for legged and humanoid robots, addressing practical challenges like gait-induced body jitter, strict payload/power constraints, and the necessity of full-surround 360-degree awareness.

Tightly integrated, hardware-aligned technical components: Features like Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) elegantly correct motion-induced phase errors at the 2D sampling coordinate stage before 3D lifting, while Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) combines Cartesian precision for near-field locomotion safety with cylindrical polar efficiency for far-field continuity.

Creation of two new benchmarks: The authors contribute 'QuadOcc' (a real quadruped 360-degree dataset with day/dusk/night coverage and semi-automatic labeling) and 'Human360Occ' (H3O, a simulated human-ego dataset), which will benefit the embodied AI community.

Comprehensive and realistic evaluation: The proposed OneOcc is compared against strong vision and LiDAR baselines. Crucially, the authors include edge-device deployment benchmarks on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, showing practical real-time viability (~13.6 FPS).

Excellent presentation and detailed ablations: The manuscript is exceptionally clear, with well-structured figures and extensive studies investigating the number of experts, horizontal field-of-view, grid choices, and calibration robustness.
weaknesses: Limited scale and diversity of the real-world dataset: Although QuadOcc is a valuable contribution, it consists of only 10 scenes in a campus environment with 6 semantic classes. Evaluation in cluttered indoor settings or highly dynamic human-populated environments would further validate real-world generalizability.

Simplified motion model for jitter: The GDC module models gait-induced jitter as a 2D translation in the projection space. While computationally efficient, this might under-parameterize high-frequency rotational vibrations (roll/pitch/yaw) during aggressive locomotion.

Reliance on 2D segmenters for ground-truth transfer: The label transfer pipeline for QuadOcc uses Grounded-SAM on unwarped equirectangular images. Panoramic distortion and seam artifacts might cause SAM to generate minor systematic segmentation boundary errors, which then propagate into the 3D ground truth.

Heuristic gating in AMoE-3D: The expert gating mechanism relies on a hand-crafted 'Gradient-Energy' function rather than a fully learned gating network. Although ablated and shown to perform well, a brief discussion or comparison with learned parametric gates would strengthen the design choice.

strengths: Addresses a novel and highly practical setting: 360-degree semantic scene completion (SSC) specifically tailored for legged and humanoid robots, handling gait-induced jitter and onboard computational constraints.

Introduces two new benchmarks (QuadOcc and Human360Occ) with multi-modal data and dense semantic occupancy ground truth, which will be of great value to the community working on embodied AI and robotics.

The proposed modules are well-designed and technically sound: Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) elegantly corrects for motion-induced phase errors in 2D before lifting; Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) combines Cartesian and cylindrical coordinates to balance near-field metric accuracy and far-field panoramic regularity.

Excellent experimental evaluation with exhaustive quantitative and qualitative results, including detailed runtime and parameter breakdowns on both desktop GPUs and embedded platforms (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin).
weaknesses: The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) simplifies the complex 6-DoF jitter of legged robots into a 2D translation offset (dx, dy) in the image plane. It is unclear how well this 2D approximation generalizes to aggressive 3D rotations (roll/pitch/yaw) or larger translation disturbances.

The parameter count of the model (101M to 189M parameters) is relatively large for resource-constrained legged robots, where memory and compute are heavily shared with real-time motion control and planning algorithms.

The dataset size of QuadOcc is somewhat limited (10 scenes, 24K frames from a single campus environment), which might restrict the generalization capability of the model in diverse real-world settings.

strengths: Addressing semantic occupancy prediction specifically for legged/humanoid robots is a highly practical and under-explored topic, particularly considering the challenges of gait-induced camera jitter and the need for full 360-degree awareness.

The proposed components are well-designed and theoretically justified: Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) elegantly resolves periodic body jitter in the 2D domain before lifting; Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) effectively leverages Cartesian coordinates for near-field accuracy and cylindrical coordinates for far-field azimuthal continuity.

The paper introduces two complementary panoramic benchmarks: QuadOcc (real-world quadruped dataset) and Human360Occ/H3O (simulated CARLA humanoid dataset). These datasets are a valuable contribution to the robotics and 3D perception communities.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations show significant improvements over state-of-the-art vision-based semantic scene completion methods, and the approach is shown to be competitive with LiDAR-based methods.

The authors provide realistic runtime and parameter analyses on an embedded edge device (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin), which is crucial for demonstrating the actual deployability of the method on physical legged robots.
weaknesses: The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) mainly targets 2D translations (particularly vertical motion blur, as detailed in Section 7 and Figure 8). However, legged locomotion often introduces complex rotational jitters (roll, pitch, and yaw) that cause non-translational spherical distortions. It is unclear how well GDC can compensate for these rotational effects.

While the method is highly optimized, the dual-projection variant on QuadOcc requires running two 2D encoders, which increases parameter count and latency. A perception throughput of ~14 FPS on AGX Orin, while impressive, might still be a bottleneck for highly agile or dynamic legged maneuvers requiring faster feedback loops.

The real-world QuadOcc dataset is relatively small (10 scenes in a campus environment), which limits the semantic diversity of the training data. However, the authors mitigate this by using the simulated H3O dataset for cross-domain evaluation.
